Earnings quality: follow the profit into cash

Use five charts to reconcile earnings, working capital, capital spending and financing, while distinguishing an analytical maintenance assumption from actual cash spent.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile one invented manufacturer’s profit, operating cash and closing cash

Interactive planning lab

Operating cash flow (CAD millions)100.0
Defined free cash flow after all cash capex (CAD millions)55.0
Closing cash / unfunded position (CAD millions)60.0

One invented manufacturing company, one common year and perimeter; all amounts are CAD millions. Each operating balance change means closing minus opening. Fixed inputs: depreciation/amortization 25 and share compensation 10 already included in net income; total cash capex 45, opening cash 40, borrowing 20, debt principal paid 30 and dividends 25. Other expensed cash outlays are assumed paid within the year. No acquisitions, disposals, FX, write-offs, reclassifications, other accruals or omitted cash flows are modeled. Operating payables exclude debt and capex creditors. The controls form conditional reconciliations, not complete financial statements or actual company data. Noncash add-backs reverse profit expenses; they are not cash receipts or proof of no economic cost. Free cash flow here means operating cash minus total cash capex, not unrestricted discretionary cash, FCFF or FCFE. The maintenance split is only an analytical assumption and cannot change cash already spent. Negative closing cash is an unfunded plan, not an available overdraft. This manufacturer template is not intended for banks or insurers. Operating cash / positive net income is 100.00%; that ratio alone is not an earnings-quality score.

The central idea

An attractive earnings multiple needs an explanation of how those earnings become cash available to owners.

01

Start with the claim you are trying to test

A company reports rising earnings, yet its cash balance is falling. That observation is a question to investigate. The business might be building inventory for signed orders, opening stores, repaying debt, or struggling to collect money from customers. Each explanation has a different implication for future earning power.

Our research approach is to write one testable sentence before building a valuation: “The company can convert its reported profit into cash after maintaining the assets required to earn it.” Then identify which disclosures would support or weaken that sentence. A low P/E alone cannot answer it.

The SEC financial-statement guide distinguishes income, cash flows, and the balance sheet. Read the statements together: profit measures a period, the balance sheet records resources and obligations at a date, and the cash-flow statement reconciles cash movements.

02

Build a bridge from net income to operating cash

Consider an invented manufacturer. Every amount below is in CAD millions and covers the same financial year. The bridge uses an indirect cash-flow presentation. It simplifies the statement to expose the main drivers.

Worked example · same year, same reporting perimeter
ComponentCash-flow adjustment
Net income100
Depreciation and amortization+25
Stock-based compensation+10
Increase in receivables−30
Increase in inventory−20
Increase in payables+15
Operating cash flow100
Cash purchases of property and equipment−45
Simplified free cash flow55

Operating cash flow equals net income here, but the business still needs 45 of capital spending. The remaining 55 is a starting point for examining financing capacity. It has not yet paid dividends, repurchased shares, completed acquisitions, or met debt principal repayments.

The stock-compensation add-back deserves separate attention. It is noncash in this period, but new shares can dilute ownership. Treating the add-back as permanently free money while assuming an unchanged share count would make the owner-return model inconsistent.

The five charts use this same manufacturer and reporting year. The noncash add-backs of 25 and 10, total cash capex of 45 and financing extension are fixed assumptions, while the controls vary net income, operating balance changes and the maintenance label. The example is not a full set of financial statements or evidence about an actual company.

03

Test the working-capital explanation

In this example, receivables and inventory absorb 50 while payables supply 15. Ask whether the 35 net cash use represents healthy expansion, deteriorating collections, or goods that may need discounting. Compare several periods and use consistent definitions.

In a separate illustration, suppose revenue rises from 800 to 1,000 while year-end receivables rise from 80 to 150. Receivables increase from 10% to 15% of annual sales. That is a useful warning flag; it does not prove customers are failing to pay. Seasonality, acquisitions, payment terms, and the timing of large invoices can all change the ratio. Average balances and credit-sales data would improve the test.

Read the receivables aging, credit-loss allowance, inventory policy, and management discussion. Compare the explanation with later collections. A working-capital release can also flatter cash flow: collecting old invoices or running down inventory can produce strong cash in a year with weak new demand.

That separate receivables/revenue case has a receivables change of 70. The main cash bridge instead uses opening receivables of 80 and closing receivables of 110, a change of 30. The new balance chart keeps the main fixture consistent, with inventory 100 to 120 and operating payables 60 to 75. A stock at a date and a change during a year are different measures.

04

A larger cash balance can come from borrowing rather than operations

The cash bridge adds a separate invented funding schedule: opening cash 40, new borrowing 20, debt principal paid 30 and dividends paid 25, all in CAD millions. Starting with operating cash of 100 and subtracting all 45 cash capex gives defined free cash flow of 55. Net financing is 20 − 30 − 25 = negative 35.

Cash therefore increases by 20 and closes at 60: 40 + 100 − 45 + 20 − 30 − 25. The operating reconciliation is used once. Neither net income nor the 55 free-cash-flow subtotal is added again on top of operating cash.

Debt principal is a financing payment, distinct from interest already represented in the operating assumptions. The model does not calculate interest, debt capacity, covenant compliance or legal dividend capacity. New borrowing can raise closing cash while leaving operating cash and this defined free cash flow unchanged.

A negative closing amount is an unfunded hypothetical plan. It identifies additional resources or changed spending needed under the assumptions, rather than an available negative bank balance. An ending cash stock must also not be confused with the year’s cash increase.

05

Separate maintenance needs from expansion claims

The 45 capital-spending figure is observable in our example. The split between maintenance and growth is an analytical judgment unless the company discloses a reliable breakdown. Calling all spending “growth investment” can overstate cash available for distribution.

Test a range. If maintaining productive capacity requires 25, cash after that requirement would be 75 before other claims. If it requires the full 45, the result is 55. Those are alternative assumptions, not two versions of reported free cash flow. Record the basis for the split rather than presenting your preferred answer as an accounting fact.

Also inspect leases, acquisitions, capitalized development, and supplier financing. The cash-flow classification can vary with the accounting framework and transaction. A consistent multi-year analysis should explain which outflows it includes and avoid comparing unlike definitions.

The maintenance control changes an analytical portion within the fixed 45 of total cash capex. At the default assumption of 25, cash after that portion is 75; the company has still paid the full 45, leaving defined free cash flow of 55. Reassigning the spending between maintenance and expansion cannot change actual closing cash in the model.

06

State what the free-cash-flow number includes

On this page, illustrative free cash flow means operating cash flow minus all cash capex of 45. It is not labeled free cash flow to the firm or free cash flow to equity, which require their own definitions and valuation conventions.

SEC staff Q102.07 explains that free cash flow is not uniformly defined and should not be presented as unrestricted discretionary cash when other claims remain. Here, debt principal and dividends already illustrate some claims that follow the operating-cash-less-capex subtotal.

The controls assume no acquisitions, disposals, currency effects, noncash balance-sheet reclassifications, write-offs or other operating accruals. Operating payables exclude debt and capex creditors. Other expensed cash outlays are paid in the same year, so the small bridge requires no additional interest or tax timing adjustment.

These limits make the sign arithmetic inspectable. They do not turn the model into an accounting template for every company. A larger cash-conversion ratio can reflect delayed supplier payments or a one-time working-capital release, while low current conversion can reflect a temporary investment in operations. Neither proves earnings quality by itself.

07

Audit adjustments before using an adjusted P/E

Management may exclude restructuring, acquisition costs, impairments, or compensation from an adjusted earnings measure. Start with the reconciliation and ask what economic activity produced each adjustment. Repeated exclusions need a reason to disappear from a future forecast.

The SEC’s non-GAAP interpretations discuss potentially misleading exclusions of recurring operating expenses and inconsistent adjustments. This is US disclosure guidance; it is not a substitute for the reporting rules that apply to a particular issuer.

For your model, preserve reported and adjusted results side by side. If reported EPS is 4.00 and adjusted EPS is 5.00, a price of 80 represents 20× reported earnings and 16× adjusted earnings. Neither denominator is automatically the right forecast anchor. Explain why an excluded cost will not recur or retain a realistic allowance for it.

08

Turn the evidence into a valuation decision

  1. Reconcile three to five years of net income, operating cash, capital spending, and share count.
  2. Identify temporary working-capital movements and test whether they later reverse.
  3. Document maintenance-spending assumptions and other contractual cash claims.
  4. Read adjusted-earnings reconciliations and identify exclusions that repeatedly return.
  5. Stress revenue, margins, collections, and funding together before selecting an earnings multiple.

A useful conclusion names both the evidence and the unresolved issue: “Cash conversion improved after collections normalized, but the maintenance-spending requirement remains uncertain.” That sentence tells the next researcher what to verify. It is more useful than a single quality score detached from the statements.

For banks and insurers, deposits, investments, regulatory capital, and financing are central to operations. Do not transfer this manufacturer’s free-cash-flow template mechanically to a financial institution. Use a framework suited to its business and capital constraints.

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios.
